analysis.title: US Economic Weekly: What's next if the Fed skips October?
key_insights: BofA keeps its call for a 25bp Fed hike in October, but says the Fed looks more inclined to hike quarterly. Williams and Jefferson leaned that way last week, and Waller's base case is hikes in Dec and Mar. Markets price only around a 20% chance of an October hike.

Benefit of pausing in October: more time to assess the data and judge the terminal rate. Cost: the Fed risks falling behind the curve with nominal GDP growing fast. BofA concludes the cons of pausing outweigh the pros.

The Fed appears worried about the long-end selloff. Jefferson said so explicitly, and Logan said the rise in term premium has done some of the tightening work. BofA is unsure whether a hike or a hold helps the long end, and argues that a decisive Fed may look more credible on inflation.

If the Fed pauses in October, BofA's most likely path is two more 25bp hikes, in Dec 2026 and Mar 2027. Risks are two-sided. Slower hikes could mean more hikes (Jun and possibly Sep 2027). Favorable 1Q base effects could instead end the cycle after December.

Markets may test the Fed's resolve to hike in December. They price about one full hike by December, and that pricing could fall sharply on soft jobs or inflation data if the Fed does not guide toward a hike.

An October hold has optics risk. The meeting is six days before the midterms, and a later decision that more hikes are needed would put the pause under scrutiny. BofA also calls the pre-data pushback from Williams and Jefferson de facto forward guidance, which sits badly with Warsh's stated objection to it.

Next week's focus is Sep CPI (Wed) and Chair Warsh's remarks at the IMF meetings. BofA expects core CPI at 0.2% m/m (2.5% y/y) and headline at 0.6% on gasoline. A 0.3% core print would put an October hike back in play.
BofA estimates Sep core PCE at 0.22% m/m and 3.0% y/y. Upside risks come from airfares, wireless service pricing and AI-related demand for electronics.

BofA raised its 3Q 2026 GDP forecast from 2.4% to 3.5% q/q saar, mostly on consumer spending (now about 3.5%). Business investment, inventories and imports also beat prior estimates, as AI capex continues to exceed expectations.
BofA lifted its 4Q/4Q 2026 growth forecast from 2.3% to 2.6%. Annual average growth rises to 2.4% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027.
The tracking estimate for 3Q GDP is unchanged at 3.5% q/q saar this week. A wider-than-expected trade deficit offset strong Sep payrolls of residential remodelers.

Fed speak this week leaned hawkish on the number of hikes but not on the pace. Musalem said rates need to rise further but showed no rush in October. The Sep minutes said most participants saw another increase as likely appropriate by year end.

Logan estimates the target range needs to rise 50bp or more. Waller floated strong forward guidance of 25bp every other meeting until 75bp of hikes are done. Bowman said she sees no urgent need for further action.

BofA's core views: growth is robust on AI capex and a resilient consumer. Core PCE is forecast at 3.1% 4Q/4Q in 2026 and stays above 2% through 2027. The labor market is roughly in balance, with payroll growth of 70k a month in 2026 and a 4.1% unemployment rate through 2027.
Card spending per household slowed to 3.0% y/y in the week ending Oct 3, possibly because of the Nor'easter. Gas spending is up 22.5% y/y, while furniture (-7.4%) and grocery (-3.4%) are weak.
BofA's rate forecasts: Fed funds 4.25-4.50% by Dec 2026 and unchanged through 2027. The 10-year Treasury yield falls from 5.23% spot to 5.00% by Dec 2026, and USD/JPY falls from 157.83 to 149.00.

Little progress on underlying inflation, which BofA sees running near 2.5%.
The spike is attributed to higher gasoline prices.
Headline inflation is accelerating on the energy shock.
Above the Fed's target but not necessarily strong enough to alter near-term policy expectations.
Strong consumer spending and AI capex point to growth well above trend, which supports the case for continued hikes.
Services activity cooled slightly and remains expansionary.

risk_factors: The Fed falls behind the curve if it pauses in October while the nominal economy booms and the energy shock passes through to core and food prices.
Y/y inflation could accelerate meaningfully over Sep-Nov because base effects are unfavorable, which would lead markets to price faster tightening and higher breakevens or term premium.
Fed credibility and independence risk, since an October pause would come six days before the midterms.
Upside inflation risks: AI-related investment, labor supply constraints from lower migration and aging, trade policy uncertainty, the Iran war and robust consumer demand.
A disorderly long-end selloff and swings in term premium before the December meeting.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 decomposes the 10-year Treasury yield into short-rate expectations and term premium, and shows the spike in long-end yields since late September has been driven by term premium.
Exhibit 2 plots core PCE inflation m/m, showing base effects are unfavorable for the next 3 months but very favorable in the six months thereafter.
vol_and_positioning: The rise in long-end Treasury yields since late September has been driven by term premium rather than short-rate expectations (Exhibit 1).
Markets price about one full Fed hike by December, and BofA thinks that pricing could come off meaningfully on soft jobs or inflation data without clear Fed guidance.
BofA says sequential hikes would probably have led markets to price in too aggressive a policy path, as they did until last week.
geopolitical: The Iran war is listed among upside risks to inflation, alongside trade policy uncertainty.
An energy shock is expected to pass through to core and food prices in coming months.

tension_points.bull_case: Hike in October: the nominal economy is booming and the energy shock may pass through to core and food prices. Hiking now, and pausing in December if October-November data allow, avoids the optics of a pause right before the midterms. A decisive Fed may also look more credible to the bond market.
tension_points.bear_case: Pause in October and hike quarterly: the Fed gets more time to assess the data and find the terminal rate. Williams, Jefferson and Waller lean this way. Logan says the rise in term premium has already done some of the tightening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 0.3% m/m core CPI print for September would put an October hike back in play. A soft Sep CPI or a Warsh signal for holding would confirm the pause.

tension_points.theme: Fed path after an October pause
tension_points.bull_case: Slower hikes could mean more hikes. The Fed might need additional moves in Jun and perhaps Sep 2027 on top of Dec 2026 and Mar 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: If y/y core inflation rolls off on favorable 1Q base effects, the Fed could stop after one more hike in Dec 2026, and markets may test its resolve to hike in December.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Soft jobs or inflation data without clear Fed guidance toward a December hike would cut the pricing of a December hike meaningfully.

theme_stances.key_argument: The cons of pausing in October outweigh the pros, given the booming nominal economy and upside inflation risks.
theme_stances.evidence: the cons of pausing outweigh the pros

theme_stances.key_argument: Relying on market-set term premium to do tightening work is uncomfortable since the Fed does not control it and it could move a lot by December.
theme_stances.evidence: The term premium argument doesn't sit comfortably with us.
